title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream, concert overture
hook: Written at seventeen after reading Shakespeare: four magic chords, whispering fairies, and a donkey’s bray.

painting.title: The Quarrel of Oberon and Titania
painting.pairingNote: Paton painted the fairy king and queen quarrelling in a moonlit wood outside Athens, crowded with tiny fairies, imps and elves, the same night world that Mendelssohn’s whispering violins conjure.

facts: In 1826, at home in Berlin, Felix Mendelssohn read Shakespeare’s *A Midsummer Night’s Dream* in the German translation by August Wilhelm Schlegel, made with help from Ludwig Tieck. At seventeen and a half he finished this overture, on 6 August that year.

It is a concert overture: a piece for the concert hall that sums up the play in music, not the prelude to a staging. It was first performed in Stettin (today Szczecin, Poland) on 20 February 1827, conducted by Carl Loewe.

Sixteen years later, King Frederick William IV of Prussia asked Mendelssohn for music for a production of the play. The overture became the first number of that incidental music, Op. 61, first heard at Potsdam in 1843, which also includes the famous *Wedding March*.
The musical scholar George Grove called the overture “the greatest marvel of early maturity that the world has ever seen in music”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: four magic chords, the fairies’ scurrying, the court of Athens, the young lovers, the clumsy workmen and a donkey’s bray, and the fairies again, who have the last word.

movements.heading: Allegro di molto
movements.summary: One movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], in which each theme stands for a group of characters from the play. Four slow chords in the woodwinds open a door into the fairy world; the violins scurry very quietly and very fast; then the full orchestra brings in the human world of the duke’s court, the lovers and the workmen. The fairies take over again, and the four chords close the door.

mainIdeas.name: The four chords
mainIdeas.description: long, soft woodwind chords, each one changing the colour a little.

mainIdeas.name: The fairies
mainIdeas.description: the violins, divided into many parts, playing quick, light notes almost in a whisper, in E minor.

mainIdeas.name: The court
mainIdeas.description: a loud, festive theme for the whole orchestra, in E major.

mainIdeas.name: The workmen and Bottom
mainIdeas.description: a clumsy dance tune, and the strings imitating a donkey’s “hee-haw” in big leaps down.

mainIdeas.name: A low voice
mainIdeas.description: the score includes an [[ophicleide|ophicleide]], a deep brass instrument with keys, which adds weight under the loud passages. Today it is often replaced by a tuba.

stops.hear: Four long, soft chords in the woodwinds, one after another
stops.happening: The magic chords: the door to the fairy world

stops.hear: The violins scurry very fast and very quietly, high up
Suddenly the whole orchestra, loud and bright
stops.happening: The court of Duke Theseus, in E major

stops.hear: A warm, longing melody in the woodwinds and strings
stops.happening: The lovers’ theme, the second theme of the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: A heavy, clumsy dance; then the strings bray in wide leaps downwards
stops.happening: The workmen, and Bottom turned into a donkey

stops.hear: Fragments of the fairy music, quiet and mysterious, wandering through new keys
stops.happening: The [[development|development]]: the fairies take over the forest

stops.hear: The four woodwind chords again, then the scurrying violins
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] begins exactly as the overture did

stops.hear: The lovers’ melody returns, followed by the workmen’s dance and the donkey’s bray
The festive court theme comes back, slow and soft, like a blessing
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]]: the fairies bless the house

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The four woodwind chords one last time, fading into silence

notice: Listen to how quiet the violins are at the start, and how long they keep it up. Mendelssohn asks for very fast, very soft playing from the whole section.
Count the four chords at the very beginning and the very end. They frame the overture like the beginning and end of a dream.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Peter Maag recorded the overture and incidental music with the London Symphony Orchestra in Kingsway Hall in February 1957. Reviewers of its CD reissue still praise the orchestra’s sparkle, though the 1957 sound is a little limited.

threads.title: A play in miniature
threads.body: Each theme is a character or a group from Shakespeare: fairies, court, lovers, workmen. The overture follows their worlds rather than the plot.

threads.title: Weber
threads.body: Carl Maria von Weber, whose fairy opera *Oberon* was first staged in London in April 1826, died that June. Mendelssohn’s overture borrows a theme from it, perhaps as a tribute.

threads.title: Sixteen years later
threads.body: When Mendelssohn wrote the rest of the music for the play in 1842–43, he took ideas from his teenage overture, such as the donkey’s bray for the workmen’s dance and the four chords for the very last moment of the play.
